questions.stem:
A 34-year-old man who moved to the United States from the Philippines 6 years ago has an interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) drawn as part of a new hospital job. The result is positive. He feels well, with no cough, fever, night sweats or weight loss. Physical examination is normal, and a chest radiograph shows clear lungs with no nodules, scarring or effusion. His coworkers ask whether they need to be tested because they shared an office with him last month.

Which of the following best describes this man's condition and what it means for his coworkers?
choices: Pulmonary tuberculosis disease, so all of his office contacts now need testing for new infection
Latent tuberculosis infection, which carries no risk of spreading the organism to contacts
Extrapulmonary tuberculosis, which is contagious only through direct contact with lesions
A false-positive result from childhood vaccination, so no further evaluation is needed
Reinfection tuberculosis, which is contagious until two negative sputum cultures return

explain.html:
Tuberculosis has two states that are easy to blur. Latent TB infection (LTBI) is the presence of M. tuberculosis without symptoms or radiographic evidence of disease; TB disease is active illness. A positive TST or IGRA shows a mature T-cell response to the organism and is a marker of infection, not of disease. Transmission needs organisms in the lung aerosolized by coughing, so LTBI is not infectious, and neither is extrapulmonary disease alone.

This man has a positive IGRA, no symptoms and a clear chest radiograph, which is LTBI. His coworkers are not contacts of an infectious case and do not need testing on his account. He still deserves evaluation and treatment of LTBI, which is how future disease is prevented.
explain.table:
LTBIPulmonary TB disease
TST or IGRAUsually positiveUsually positive (may be negative if very ill)
SymptomsNoneCough 3 weeks or more, fever, night sweats, weight loss
Chest radiographNormalUsually abnormal
InfectiousNoYes
why: Pulmonary disease would usually bring symptoms or radiographic findings, and he has neither.
Nothing suggests an extrapulmonary site, and extrapulmonary TB without lung disease is not infectious by any route.
IGRAs are not affected by BCG vaccination, so the result cannot be dismissed that way.
Reinfection is rare outside advanced immune deficiency, and there is no disease here to transmit.
explain.takeaway: Latent TB infection is a positive TST or IGRA without symptoms or radiographic disease, and it is not infectious.
explain.topic: Latent TB infection vs TB disease
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Understand Tuberculosis Terms: LTBI vs. TB Disease

questions.stem:
A county health department is ranking four newly reported patients to decide which contact investigation to start first. Patient 1 has tuberculous lymphadenitis of the neck with a normal chest radiograph. Patient 2 has a positive tuberculin skin test and no symptoms. Patient 3 has a 2-month cough, a cavity in the right upper lobe and sputum smears showing many acid-fast bacilli. Patient 4 has culture-proven pulmonary TB and completed 4 weeks of effective therapy with a resolving cough.

Patient 3 is the most likely to have transmitted infection because of which of the following?
choices: Cavitary disease carries a high organism burden that coughing aerosolizes
Lymph node disease releases organisms into the blood that reach the airways
Cavitary organisms are more often drug resistant and therefore more infectious
Smear-positive patients shed large respiratory droplets that settle on surfaces
Skin test reactivity in this patient indicates the strain is highly virulent

explain.html:
TB spreads person to person through the air in tiny droplet nuclei of 1 to 10 micrometers, which stay airborne and travel long distances; environmental surfaces carry minimal risk. Only pulmonary TB disease is infectious, and even then risk varies. Infectiousness depends on the number of organisms in the lung and how effectively they are aerosolized, mainly by coughing. Markers of more lung organisms are a positive AFB sputum smear and cavities on imaging. Room size, ventilation and length of exposure also matter, and infectiousness falls rapidly on effective treatment.

Patient 3 has a 2-month cough, a right upper lobe cavity and smears full of acid-fast bacilli, so he combines a high organism burden with coughing. The node disease and the positive skin test alone are not infectious, and Patient 4's risk has dropped on therapy. His contacts come first.
explain.table:
PatientInfectious?Why
1, lymph node TBNoExtrapulmonary without lung disease
2, positive TST onlyNoLTBI
3, cavity, smear positive, coughHighestHigh lung burden, aerosolized by cough
4, 4 weeks of therapyFallingInfectiousness drops on effective treatment
why: Lymph node TB without pulmonary disease is not infectious.
Resistance is not what makes a patient infectious; organism burden and aerosolization are.
TB spreads by tiny airborne droplet nuclei, not large droplets, and surfaces carry minimal risk.
A skin test measures the host's T-cell response, not the virulence of the organism.
explain.takeaway: TB transmission risk rises with pulmonary disease that has a high organism burden (positive smear, cavities) plus coughing, and falls rapidly on effective treatment.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
Five adults have tuberculin skin tests (TST) placed and read at 48 to 72 hours. None has symptoms or an abnormal chest radiograph. Their induration and history are: (A) 8 mm, an office accountant with no known TB risk factors; (B) 12 mm, a software engineer with no known TB risk factors; (C) 6 mm, a man with HIV infection; (D) 7 mm, a nursing home employee; (E) 9 mm, a man who arrived from a high-incidence country 2 years ago.

Which of these results should be read as positive?
choices: The accountant with 8 mm
The software engineer with 12 mm
The man with HIV and 6 mm
The nursing home employee with 7 mm
The recent immigrant with 9 mm

explain.html:
The tuberculin skin test is read as millimeters of induration at 48 to 72 hours, and what counts as positive depends on the population. A smaller threshold increases sensitivity, so it is used where missing an infection is most dangerous. 5 mm applies to HIV infection, close contacts of an infectious case, old untreated TB on radiograph, transplant recipients and other immune suppression. 10 mm applies to recent immigrants, people who inject drugs, residents and employees of congregate settings, health care workers and children under 4. 15 mm applies to people with no known TB risk.

The man with HIV has 6 mm, which clears his 5 mm cutoff. The nursing home employee (7 mm) and the immigrant (9 mm) fall short of 10 mm, and the two people with no risk factors fall short of 15 mm. Matching each person to a cutoff before reading the number avoids the trap of calling the biggest reaction positive.
explain.table:
CutoffWho
5 mm or moreHIV, close contact of an infectious case, old untreated TB on radiograph, organ transplant, other immune suppression (TNF-alpha inhibitor, prednisone over 15 mg a day for a month), suspected TB disease
10 mm or moreRecent immigrants, people who inject drugs, congregate settings (jails, nursing homes), health care and mycobacteriology lab workers, children under 4
15 mm or moreNo known TB risk
why: With no risk factors the cutoff is 15 mm, so 8 mm is negative.
With no risk factors the cutoff is 15 mm, so 12 mm is negative despite being the largest reading.
Congregate-setting employees use a 10 mm cutoff, so 7 mm is negative.
Recent immigrants use a 10 mm cutoff, so 9 mm is negative.
explain.takeaway: The TST cutoff (5, 10 or 15 mm) is set by the person's risk, with 5 mm used for the highest-risk groups such as HIV infection.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: TB Diagnostic tests- for TB infection (and TB Disease*)

rows.if_right: an 8 mm reaction in a person with HIV or a close contact of an infectious case

rows.why: With no risk factors the cutoff is 15 mm, so 12 mm is negative despite being the largest reading.
rows.if_right: a 12 mm reaction in a recent immigrant or health care worker

rows.why: Congregate-setting employees use a 10 mm cutoff, so 7 mm is negative.
rows.if_right: a 7 mm reaction in a nursing home employee who is on a TNF-alpha inhibitor

rows.if_right: a reaction of 10 mm or more in the same recent immigrant

questions.stem:
A 26-year-old woman from Ethiopia starts nursing school in New Jersey and needs testing for tuberculosis infection. She received a vaccine at birth that left a small scar on her upper arm. She has no symptoms. A previous tuberculin skin test placed in her home country was read as 13 mm, and she was told it was probably due to the vaccine. She lives 90 minutes from campus and would have difficulty returning for a second visit.

Which of the following is the best test to evaluate her for tuberculosis infection?
choices: Repeat tuberculin skin test read at 48 to 72 hours
Two-step tuberculin skin test placed one to three weeks apart
Interferon-gamma release assay on a single blood sample
Three sputum samples for acid-fast stain and culture
Chest computed tomography as the initial screening test

explain.html:
BCG is a modified M. bovis strain given where TB incidence is high to prevent overwhelming disease in infants and children. It stimulates cell-mediated immunity to TB and can cause a positive TST, although the effect often wanes over time. An IGRA measures interferon-gamma from antigen-specific T cells, is not affected by BCG or most NTM, and needs only one visit, while the TST needs two or more. The rule for choosing a test is IGRA if prior BCG, or low likelihood to return for a TST reading.

She has a vaccination scar from birth, a prior 13 mm TST that cannot be separated from a BCG effect, and a 90-minute trip that makes a return visit unlikely. Both features point to an IGRA. Sputum testing is for suspected disease, which she does not have.
explain.table:
TSTIGRA
Visits2 or moreOne
Prior BCGPossible false positiveNot affected
NTMPossible false positiveMost do not cause one
Booster reactionYesShould not occur
ReadingSubjectiveDone in lab
Negative resultDoes not exclude TBDoes not exclude TB
why: A repeat skin test still cannot separate a BCG effect from infection and needs a return visit she is unlikely to make.
Two-step testing addresses boosting, not BCG cross-reactivity, and needs even more visits.
Sputum testing looks for TB disease, and she has no symptoms.
CT is not recommended as an initial screening test for those being evaluated for TB.
explain.takeaway: BCG can cause a false-positive TST, so an IGRA is preferred in anyone with prior BCG or who may not return for a TST reading.
explain.topic: BCG vaccination and choice of TB test
explain.subject: Microbiology

rows.if_right: a person with no BCG history who can easily return in 48 to 72 hours

questions.stem:
A 63-year-old man who emigrated from Vietnam 30 years ago is hired at a long-term care facility. His baseline tuberculin skin test shows 3 mm of induration. Per facility policy, a second skin test is placed 2 weeks later and shows 14 mm. He has no symptoms, no known exposure to anyone with tuberculosis during those 2 weeks, and a normal chest radiograph.

Which of the following best explains the change between his two skin test results?
choices: He acquired a new tuberculosis infection in the two weeks between tests
The second reading was falsely raised by an infection with an environmental mycobacterium
Antibodies formed against the first tuberculin dose cross-reacted with the second
The first test recalled a waned T-cell response to an infection from years ago
The tuberculin from the first test caused active disease that reacted with the second

explain.html:
Some people infected long ago have a negative TST because their T-cell response has waned over the years. The antigens in that first test can boost the reaction, so a second TST placed soon after is positive. Read on its own, that second result can be misinterpreted as a new infection (a conversion) rather than a boosted reaction. That is why two-step testing is done at baseline for people, such as health care workers, who will be tested repeatedly.

He emigrated 30 years ago, his first test was 3 mm and the second, two weeks later, was 14 mm, with no exposure in between and a normal radiograph. That pattern is a boosted response to remote infection, and his true baseline is the second result. IGRAs should not show a booster reaction.
why: He had no exposure in the two weeks, and the pattern after a first test fits boosting rather than conversion.
Some NTM can cause a false-positive TST, but that does not explain a jump right after a first test.
The TST reads a T-cell (delayed-type) response, not antibody.
Tuberculin is a purified protein derivative and cannot cause infection or disease.
explain.takeaway: Remote TB infection can give a falsely negative first TST that boosts on retesting, so two-step testing prevents a boosted reaction from being read as a new conversion.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: TB Diagnostic tests- for TB infection (and TB Disease*)

rows.if_right: a documented negative two-step baseline followed by a positive test after a known exposure

rows.if_right: a positive TST with a negative IGRA in someone with NTM exposure

rows.why: The TST reads a T-cell (delayed-type) response, not antibody.
rows.if_right: a serologic assay, which reads circulating antibody rather than a T-cell response

rows.if_right: a live vaccine strain such as BCG, not a purified skin test reagent

questions.stem:
A 41-year-old woman from Haiti has a positive interferon-gamma release assay on routine screening before starting a job at a correctional facility. On questioning she reports 5 weeks of a productive cough, drenching night sweats and a 4 kg weight loss. Temperature is 38.1 C (100.6 F). Chest radiograph shows patchy opacities in the right upper lobe. Her clinician had planned to start treatment for latent infection.

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
choices: Start the planned latent-infection treatment and repeat the chest radiograph in 3 months
Repeat the interferon-gamma release assay to confirm the result before acting
Collect three sputum samples for smear and culture plus a nucleic acid test
Place a tuberculin skin test to decide whether the assay was a false positive
Start isoniazid alone for 9 months because her symptoms suggest a higher burden

explain.html:
Everyone with a positive TB test is evaluated for disease with a history, physical exam and chest radiograph. If there are symptoms or an abnormal CXR, testing must exclude active disease: three sputum specimens at least 8 hours apart for AFB smear and culture, plus at least one NAAT. Pulmonary TB symptoms include a productive cough of 3 weeks or more, chest pain and hemoptysis, with systemic fever, night sweats and weight loss. The lecture is explicit: do not treat for LTBI if there is concern for TB disease, and treatment of disease is always combination therapy.

She has 5 weeks of productive cough, night sweats, weight loss, fever and right upper lobe opacities. That is suspected pulmonary TB, so the planned latent-infection treatment must wait while sputum is collected.
why: Latent-infection treatment must not be given when disease is suspected, and she has symptoms and an abnormal film.
Repeating the assay adds nothing; the question is disease, which immune tests cannot answer.
Doing both TST and IGRA is not routinely recommended, and neither separates infection from disease.
Treatment of TB disease is always combination therapy, so one drug is never adequate here.
explain.takeaway: After a positive TST or IGRA, symptoms or an abnormal chest radiograph require sputum smears, cultures and a NAAT, and LTBI is never treated when disease is suspected.
explain.subject: Microbiology

rows.why: Latent-infection treatment must not be given when disease is suspected, and she has symptoms and an abnormal film.
rows.if_right: a positive IGRA with no symptoms and a normal chest radiograph

rows.why: Repeating the assay adds nothing; the question is disease, which immune tests cannot answer.
rows.if_right: an indeterminate or borderline first IGRA in a well person

questions.stem:
A TB clinic has enough staff to start latent infection treatment in only one patient this week. All five have a positive interferon-gamma release assay, no symptoms and no evidence of active disease. Patient A is a 30-year-old smoker. Patient B is a 45-year-old with well-controlled type 2 diabetes. Patient C is a 52-year-old with chronic kidney disease. Patient D is a 27-year-old who is 8% below ideal body weight. Patient E is a 38-year-old with untreated HIV infection and a low CD4 count.

Which patient has the highest risk of progressing to TB disease?
choices: Patient A, the smoker
Patient B, with diabetes
Patient C, with kidney disease
Patient D, who is underweight
Patient E, with untreated HIV infection

explain.html:
Evaluating a positive TB test has a goal beyond finding disease: identify LTBI with a higher risk of progression, because those people gain the most from treatment and get the highest priority. Latent infection stays latent because T-cell immunity contains it, so conditions that weaken immunity raise the risk. The lecture's ranking puts advanced, untreated HIV infection at the top (relative risk about 10), followed by recent close contact with infectious TB (6.1) and an old healed, never treated TB scar on CXR (5.2). Below them are prednisone over 15 mg a day, chronic renal failure (2.4), TNF-alpha inhibitors, poorly controlled diabetes (1.7), malnutrition over 10% under ideal weight (1.6) and smoking (1.5).

Patient E's untreated HIV with a low CD4 count dwarfs the others. Patient D is only 8% underweight, below the malnutrition threshold, and B's diabetes is well controlled. Treat Patient E first.
explain.table:
Risk factorRelative risk
Advanced, untreated HIV9.5 to 9.9
Close contact with infectious TB6.1
Old healed TB on CXR, never treated5.2
Prednisone over 15 mg/day for over 2 weeks2.8
Chronic renal failure2.4
TNF-alpha inhibitor2.0 or more
Poorly controlled diabetes1.7
Malnutrition (over 10% under ideal weight)1.6
Smoking1.5
why: Smoking carries the lowest listed relative risk, about 1.5.
Diabetes raises risk modestly (1.7) and mainly when poorly controlled, and hers is well controlled.
Chronic renal failure raises risk only about 2.4 times, far below untreated HIV.
Malnutrition counts only above 10% under ideal weight, so 8% does not even meet the definition.
explain.takeaway: Advanced untreated HIV is the strongest risk factor for progression from latent TB infection to disease, followed by recent close contact and an untreated old TB scar.
explain.topic: Risk of progression from LTBI to disease
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 36-year-old woman from India who takes a tumor necrosis factor alpha inhibitor for Crohn disease develops a painless, slowly enlarging mass on the side of her neck over 2 months, with low-grade fevers. Fine-needle aspiration shows caseating granulomas, and culture grows Mycobacterium tuberculosis. She has no cough, and chest radiograph is normal. She lives with her husband and two school-age children and asks whether her family is at risk of catching TB from her.

Which of the following is the most accurate statement about her illness?
choices: Her household should wear masks until she has completed 2 weeks of treatment
Organisms draining from the node can spread the infection through shared towels
She cannot transmit infection, because she has no disease in her lungs
Her children need sputum testing because lymph node TB spreads easily to children
She most likely acquired this infection from contaminated food rather than air

explain.html:
About 70% of US TB cases are pulmonary only, 18% are extrapulmonary only and 11% are both, and among extrapulmonary sites lymphatic disease is the most common. Extrapulmonary TB is more frequent in the immune suppressed, including people on TNF inhibitors and with HIV, and its diagnosis is often late because specimens are harder to get. Transmission requires organisms in the lung aerosolized by coughing, so extrapulmonary TB without pulmonary TB is non-infectious. Surfaces carry minimal risk.

She has a cervical node with caseating granulomas growing M. tuberculosis, no cough and a normal chest radiograph, and she takes a TNF-alpha inhibitor. Her family cannot catch TB from her, because there is no lung disease to aerosolize. Household members may still be evaluated because they may share her exposures, not as contacts of an infectious case.
why: Masking is for infectious pulmonary disease, which she does not have.
Environmental surfaces carry minimal TB risk, and transmission is airborne from the lungs.
Lymph node TB does not spread person to person, so her children are not her contacts.
M. tuberculosis has human reservoirs and spreads by airborne droplet nuclei, not food.
explain.takeaway: Extrapulmonary TB, most often lymphatic, is more frequent with immune suppression such as TNF inhibitors and is not infectious without pulmonary disease.
explain.subject: Microbiology

rows.why: Masking is for infectious pulmonary disease, which she does not have.
rows.if_right: a patient with smear-positive cavitary lung disease and cough

rows.why: Environmental surfaces carry minimal TB risk, and transmission is airborne from the lungs.
rows.if_right: an organism that persists on fomites, such as Enterococcus on hospital surfaces

rows.why: Lymph node TB does not spread person to person, so her children are not her contacts.
rows.if_right: a child living with an adult who has infectious pulmonary TB

rows.why: M. tuberculosis has human reservoirs and spreads by airborne droplet nuclei, not food.
rows.if_right: infection from drinking unpasteurized milk from tuberculous cows (M. bovis)

questions.stem:
A 67-year-old man from China has a positive interferon-gamma release assay. He reports a mild cough for 6 weeks and a 3 kg weight loss. He says he was treated for tuberculosis as a teenager. Chest radiograph shows fibrotic scarring with volume loss in the left upper lobe and a few calcified nodules. No earlier films are available for comparison. His clinician wants to decide whether he needs further testing.

Which of the following is the correct interpretation of his chest radiograph?
choices: It cannot distinguish old healed TB from active disease, so sputum testing is needed
It shows only inactive scarring, which rules out active disease without any further testing
It shows calcified nodules, which confirm reactivation and justify treatment alone
It is less sensitive than the skin test, so a tuberculin test should replace it
It confirms nontuberculous mycobacterial disease because of the fibrotic pattern

explain.html:
The chest radiograph has a clear role and a clear limit. A normal CXR with no symptoms makes pulmonary TB very unlikely, although TB can occur with a negative film and symptoms may be subtle. CT is more sensitive but is not the initial screening test. Most important, a CXR cannot distinguish inactive, old healed TB from active pulmonary TB. So anyone with symptoms or an abnormal film after a positive test needs sputum smears, cultures and NAATs.

He has 6 weeks of cough, weight loss, a positive IGRA and left upper lobe fibrosis with calcified nodules, with no old films for comparison. The scarring might be from his teenage TB, or the disease might be active again, and the film cannot tell which. Sputum testing settles it.
why: Scarring cannot be called inactive on a film alone, especially in a man with cough and weight loss.
A radiograph cannot establish active disease by itself, and treatment of disease begins after specimens are sent.
Immune-based tests measure infection, which his IGRA already shows; they do not assess disease.
A radiograph cannot identify the species, and NTM manifestations overlap with TB.
explain.takeaway: A chest radiograph cannot distinguish old healed TB from active TB, so symptoms or an abnormal film require sputum smear, culture and NAAT.
explain.subject: Microbiology

rows.why: Scarring cannot be called inactive on a film alone, especially in a man with cough and weight loss.
rows.if_right: a well person with no symptoms whose current film matches an unchanged older film

rows.why: A radiograph cannot establish active disease by itself, and treatment of disease begins after specimens are sent.
rows.if_right: a very ill patient with high suspicion, started on therapy right after sputum is collected

rows.why: Immune-based tests measure infection, which his IGRA already shows; they do not assess disease.
rows.if_right: a well person being screened for TB infection, where TST or IGRA is the test

rows.if_right: culture identifying a nontuberculous mycobacterium

questions.stem:
A 3-year-old boy is evaluated 2 months after his grandfather, who lives in the same apartment, was diagnosed with smear-positive cavitary pulmonary tuberculosis. The boy has had a cough and poor weight gain for 4 weeks. Chest radiograph shows enlarged hilar lymph nodes and a right middle lobe opacity. He cannot produce sputum on request, and the team wants a specimen for acid-fast smear, culture and nucleic acid testing.

Which of the following is the preferred way to obtain a specimen in this child?
choices: Lumbar puncture for cerebrospinal fluid
Blood culture drawn into mycobacterial media
Urine sample collected on three mornings
Throat swab from the posterior pharynx
Early-morning gastric aspiration

explain.html:
Diagnosis of pulmonary TB rests on sputum: three specimens at least 8 hours apart for AFB smear and culture, plus at least one NAAT, collected with airborne precautions. When a patient cannot cough up a quality specimen, the options are sputum induction with nebulized saline, bronchoscopy or gastric aspiration. Gastric aspiration is preferred in infants and younger children. Very young children have a high risk of disease after infection, and diagnosis is harder in them.

This 3-year-old lives with a grandfather who has smear-positive cavitary TB and now has cough, poor weight gain, hilar adenopathy and a lung opacity. He cannot produce sputum, so an early-morning gastric aspirate is the specimen to send. The other choices do not sample the lungs.
explain.table:
Can the patient produce sputum?Specimen
Yes3 sputum samples at least 8 hours apart, plus NAAT
No, adult or older childSputum induction with nebulized saline or bronchoscopy
No, infant or young childGastric aspiration (preferred)
why: There are no signs of meningitis, and spinal fluid does not sample the lungs.
Blood culture is not among the specimen options for suspected pulmonary TB.
Urine samples the genitourinary tract, not the lungs.
A throat swab does not sample the lower respiratory tract and is not a listed option.
explain.takeaway: When sputum cannot be produced, options are induction, bronchoscopy or gastric aspiration, and gastric aspiration is preferred in infants and young children.
explain.subject: Microbiology

rows.why: There are no signs of meningitis, and spinal fluid does not sample the lungs.
rows.if_right: a child with suspected meningeal TB

rows.why: Blood culture is not among the specimen options for suspected pulmonary TB.
rows.if_right: advanced HIV with disseminated MAC spreading to the bone marrow, not a lung specimen

rows.why: Urine samples the genitourinary tract, not the lungs.
rows.if_right: suspected genitourinary TB

rows.why: A throat swab does not sample the lower respiratory tract and is not a listed option.
rows.if_right: an upper airway infection sampled from the throat

questions.stem:
A 58-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis was started on a biologic agent 5 months ago after methotrexate failed. She now has 3 weeks of fever and night sweats. Chest radiograph shows a miliary pattern, and a biopsy of an enlarged lymph node shows poorly formed granulomas with many acid-fast bacilli. Before therapy began, her tuberculin skin test was 7 mm, which was not acted on. She grew up in a country where tuberculosis is common.

The biologic agent most likely allowed disease by interfering with which of the following?
choices: Production of neutralizing antibody that blocks bacillary entry into macrophages
A cytokine that holds infected macrophages in a contained structure
Complement-mediated lysis of the waxy mycobacterial cell wall
Neutrophil degranulation that kills bacilli in the alveolar space
Mucociliary clearance that removes inhaled droplet nuclei

explain.html:
After infection, most people control M. tuberculosis as specific T-cell mediated immunity develops, and the organism is held in the granuloma. Mycobacteria are intracellular pathogens of macrophages: dendritic cells make IL-12, which drives Th1 cells, and Th1 cells make interferon-gamma, which activates macrophages, while IL-2 supports cytotoxic T cells. The lecture stresses the consequences of cytokine inhibitors, and its risk table lists treatment with a TNF-alpha inhibitor as a risk for progression from LTBI to disease. Lifelong reactivation risk rises whenever local or systemic immune function weakens.

Her pretreatment TST of 7 mm was already positive for someone about to start immune suppression (5 mm cutoff), so she had LTBI that was never treated. Five months on a biologic, she has miliary disease with poorly formed granulomas full of bacilli, the picture of a granuloma that lost its cytokine support. Screen and treat LTBI before starting these drugs.
why: Antibody is not the main defense against an organism that lives inside macrophages; control is cell mediated.
Containment of TB depends on T cells and macrophages in granulomas, not complement lysis of the waxy wall.
Neutrophils are not the cells that hold latent TB; Th1 cytokines and activated macrophages do.
Mucociliary clearance acts at first exposure, not in reactivation of an established latent infection.
explain.takeaway: Cell-mediated immunity (IL-12, interferon-gamma, TNF-alpha) holds TB in granulomas, so TNF-alpha inhibitors raise the risk of progression from latent infection to disease.

questions.stem:
A 29-year-old man with advanced HIV infection (CD4 count 40 cells/microL, normal 500 to 1,500) presents with 6 weeks of fever, weight loss and cough. Chest radiograph shows innumerable tiny nodules throughout both lungs. Sputum smear shows acid-fast bacilli, and a nucleic acid amplification test detects Mycobacterium tuberculosis. A tuberculin skin test placed on admission shows 0 mm of induration, and an interferon-gamma release assay returns indeterminate.

Which of the following best explains the skin test and blood assay results?
choices: The organism lacks the antigens that both tests are designed to detect
Prior BCG vaccination has blocked the response that both tests measure
High circulating antibody levels have neutralized the test antigens
Too few T cells remain to mount the cell-mediated response that both tests measure
The organisms are confined to granulomas and cannot reach the test site

explain.html:
The TST and IGRA are different ways of measuring the same response: both measure the host immune response to TB, not the organism. The TST reads delayed-type hypersensitivity to injected PPD, and the IGRA requires antigen-specific CD4 or CD8 cells to release interferon-gamma. So both fail when the response fails: TST false negatives come from anergy, very recent infection and severe TB disease, and IGRAs may be indeterminate or falsely negative with impaired immunity or severe disease. For both, a negative result does not exclude TB infection or disease.

He has a CD4 count of 40 and disseminated disease confirmed by smear and NAAT, yet 0 mm on TST and an indeterminate IGRA. Too few working T cells explain both results. Disease is diagnosed with smears, cultures and NAATs, not immune tests.
why: The organism is confirmed M. tuberculosis, which carries the antigens both tests use.
BCG can make a TST falsely positive, not negative, and does not affect IGRAs.
Neither test depends on antibody; both read T-cell responses.
He has disseminated disease, not contained infection, and both tests read circulating T cells.
explain.takeaway: The TST and IGRA measure the T-cell response, so immune suppression or severe TB disease can make them falsely negative or indeterminate, and a negative result never excludes TB.

questions.stem:
A state health department notes that its TB case count has fallen slowly for a decade, and that nearly 90% of new cases occur in people born in high-incidence countries, many of whom were diagnosed years after arriving. Contact investigations and treatment of every active case are already in place. Planners want the single strategy most likely to move the state toward TB elimination.

Which strategy best fits this goal?
choices: Vaccinating all infants with BCG to prevent overwhelming childhood disease
Screening at-risk groups for infection and treating those infected before disease
Restricting screening to patients who report cough lasting more than 3 weeks
Repeating chest radiographs every year in all residents born outside the US
Placing every person with a positive IGRA in airborne isolation until cleared

explain.html:
About a quarter of the world's population has been infected with TB, and the public health strategy depends on local incidence. High-incidence, often resource-limited regions mainly treat TB disease and some highest-risk infected people, with little screening, aiming for TB control. Low-incidence regions such as the US treat disease and screen for and treat infection, aiming for elimination. In the US, non-US-born people now account for most cases, often presenting many years after arrival; New Jersey's foreign-born share was 87.5% in 2023.

Here nearly 90% of cases occur in people born abroad and diagnosed years later, so the cases come from reactivation of latent infection, not new local spread. Treating active cases cannot reach that pool. Elimination where incidence is low is only achievable by treating those infected before they develop TB disease.
explain.table:
High incidenceLow incidence (US)
ResourcesOften limitedUsually higher
StrategyTreat disease and some highest-risk infected; little screeningTreat disease and screen and treat most infected
GoalControl, then eliminationElimination
why: BCG is used where incidence is high to prevent overwhelming disease in infants, and it gives no benefit after age 10, so it cannot stop adult reactivation.
Waiting for cough finds disease only, not the latent pool that feeds future cases.
Radiographs are normal in latent infection, so yearly films miss the pool to be treated.
Latent infection is not infectious and does not need isolation.
explain.takeaway: In low-incidence settings most TB comes from reactivation, so elimination requires screening for and treating latent infection.
explain.topic: TB control strategy in low vs high incidence settings

questions.stem:
A 34-year-old nurse starting a new hospital job has a positive interferon-gamma release assay on pre-employment screening. She was born in a country with high TB incidence, received BCG as an infant, and has a BCG scar. Four years ago, after a positive test, she completed a full, documented course of treatment for latent TB infection. Since then she has had no known TB exposure. She has no cough, fever, night sweats or weight loss, and her chest radiograph is normal. Her HIV test is negative. Occupational health asks whether this result means something new has happened.

Which of the following best explains her positive result?
choices: Her infant BCG vaccine is producing a false-positive interferon-gamma result
A memory T-cell response that persists even after effective treatment
Prior skin testing boosted her response, so the assay now reads positive
Exposure to environmental mycobacteria that cross-react with the assay antigens
The earlier latent infection treatment failed and organisms are now multiplying

explain.html:
The TST and IGRAs are different ways of measuring the same response: both detect a mature, antigen-specific T-cell response to M. tuberculosis, not the organism itself. That is why both tests remain positive after treatment. The two tests differ in their pitfalls. The TST can be falsely positive after BCG or some NTM infections and can show boosting on repeat testing, while the IGRA is not affected by BCG, should not boost, and is not made positive by most NTM.

This nurse had documented, completed LTBI treatment four years ago and has no new exposure, no symptoms and a normal chest radiograph. Her positive IGRA is the expected memory response to that old infection, not a sign of a new infection or of treatment failure. The BCG scar is the trap, because BCG confounds the TST but not the IGRA. The practical point is that repeating a TB test after treatment cannot show cure, and a positive test in someone already treated calls for a symptom review and radiograph rather than retreatment.
explain.table:
FeatureTSTIGRA
Prior BCGPossible false positiveNot affected
Most NTMPossible false positiveUsually no false positive
Booster reactionYesShould not occur
After treatmentRemains positiveRemains positive
why: BCG can cause a false-positive TST, but the IGRA is not affected by prior BCG vaccination.
Boosting occurs when one TST recalls a waned response on a later TST; an IGRA should not show a booster reaction.
Most nontuberculous mycobacteria do not make the IGRA positive; NTM cross-reaction is mainly a TST issue.
Failed treatment would mean TB disease, and she has no symptoms and a normal radiograph; the assay measures immunity, not organisms.
explain.takeaway: Both the TST and IGRA measure a T-cell response to M. tuberculosis antigens and remain positive after successful treatment, and the IGRA is not affected by BCG or boosting.

questions.stem:
A 3-year-old girl is evaluated 10 days after her father was diagnosed with cavitary pulmonary tuberculosis with a sputum smear showing many acid-fast bacilli. The child lives in a small apartment with him and has slept in his room for the past month. She received BCG at birth while the family lived abroad. She is active and eating well, with no cough or fever. Her chest radiograph is normal and her HIV test is negative. A tuberculin skin test read at 72 hours shows 2 mm of induration. Her mother is relieved and asks whether this result means the child escaped infection.

Which of the following is the best interpretation of the skin test?
choices: It is negative, because 2 mm falls below the 5 mm cutoff set for any close contact
It is reassuring, because infant BCG prevents infection in children under 5
It may be falsely negative, as T cells may not yet react to a very new infection
It is reassuring, because young children rarely become infected from adult TB cases
It is falsely negative, because BCG suppresses the reaction to tuberculin

explain.html:
After inhaled M. tuberculosis reaches the lung of a TB-naive person, the bacteria replicate and spread locally while specific T-cell immunity evolves; a positive TST or IGRA indicates a mature T-cell response and is the marker of infection. Because that response takes time to develop, very recent infection is listed among the causes of a false-negative TST, along with anergy and severe TB disease. A negative result therefore does not exclude infection.

This child had close, prolonged exposure to a highly infectious source (cavitary disease with a positive AFB smear), and she was tested only 10 days after his diagnosis. Her 2 mm result is exactly what a just-acquired infection could look like. The BCG history is the trap: infant BCG reduces the risk of disease under age 5 by about 37 percent but does not prevent infection, and it causes false-positive, not false-negative, skin tests. Since children under 5 have a high risk of progressing to disease after infection, her negative test cannot be taken as reassurance.
explain.table:
TST result problemCauses
False positiveBCG vaccination, some NTM
False negativeAnergy, very recent infection, severe TB disease
why: The 5 mm cutoff is correct for a close contact, but a reading taken soon after exposure can be negative despite infection.
Infant BCG lowers the risk of TB disease under age 5 by about a third; it does not prevent infection.
Infants and young children have a high risk of infection and disease after exposure, and this source is highly infectious.
BCG stimulates cell-mediated immunity to mycobacteria and causes false-positive skin tests, not false negatives.
explain.takeaway: A false-negative tuberculin skin test can occur with very recent infection because the test requires a mature T-cell response, so a negative test soon after exposure does not exclude infection.
